Restores the source's population (asymptomatic AF) and its scope (a model applied to a single ECG at the point of care), as citation report C70 and C71 give.
ops.new_text: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common arrhythmia, and in people with asymptomatic AF the first presentation may be a stroke or heart failure \cite{Kashou_2021}. In the Framingham Study, AF was associated with a near fivefold excess of stroke. The stroke risk attributable to AF rose from 1.5\% at ages 50 to 59 to 23.5\% at ages 80 to 89 \cite{Wolf_1991}. Over 50 years of the same cohort, the age-adjusted prevalence of AF rose about fourfold and its incidence more than tripled, in part through more intensive surveillance \cite{Schnabel_2015}. Identifying the people who will develop AF could therefore guide monitoring before a first complication. Clinical risk scores such as CHARGE-AF estimate this risk from routine variables \cite{Alonso_2013}. These scores need the abstraction of clinical data, which takes time, whereas a model applied to a single ECG at the point of care needs no additional data abstraction \cite{Kashou_2021}. The resting 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is thus a candidate source of risk information in its own right.

ops.rationale: Words the opening as new-onset AF (C88) and moves the guideline sentence, reworded to automated AF diagnosis, out of the new-onset results into 1.2 (C72).
ops.new_text: Deep networks trained on sinus-rhythm ECGs predict new-onset AF. A network trained on 1.6 million ECGs reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.85 for new-onset AF within one year \cite{Raghunath_2021}. When an ECG network and CHARGE-AF were combined, discrimination was highest for the combination in an internal and two external test sets \cite{Khurshid_2022}. The ECG and the clinical risk factors therefore carry partly different information. Reported performance also depends on how the outcome is defined. A systematic review of 14 studies found a median AUC of 0.740, with higher values for 31-day confirmation windows than for 1-year windows (0.851 against 0.630) \cite{Tsiartas_2025}. Eleven of these studies cited possible misclassification of negative cases. A model of incident AF therefore has to be judged with its outcome window and its label source stated.

ops.rationale: Rests the commentary sentence on the title the record holds (C67), places the guideline statement on automated AF diagnosis beside the point on clinical use (C72), and restores the hedge 'for most methods' (C73).
ops.new_text: The networks behind these results are black boxes, and their explanations are computed after training. A commentary on predicting incident AF in sinus rhythm is subtitled ``more than just trusting the `black box'\,'' \cite{Kashou_2021}, and a narrative review names interpretability as a barrier to clinical use \cite{Saiz_Vivo_2025}. The 2024 guideline of the European Society of Cardiology addresses the neighbouring task of automated AF diagnosis. It states that the clinical performance and broad applicability of such algorithms are not yet known \cite{Van_Gelder_2024}. The explanations themselves are uncertain. Twelve attribution methods applied to ECG classifiers agreed poorly and were only moderately consistent across training runs for most methods \cite{Arends_2026}. For some of these methods, randomising the weights of the network did not remove the attribution pattern entirely. An explanation of this kind may describe the attribution method as much as the model. Rudin argued that a model for high-stakes decisions should be interpretable by design, instead of a black box explained afterwards \cite{Rudin_2019}. For incident AF, such a model would have to keep the discrimination of a deep network while exposing what it reads from the ECG.

ops.rationale: States what Ye_2020 does (Grad-CAM explanation, C74) and what Faes_2024 reports (BTTR designed for interpretability predicted finger movements, C75); the linear, non-survival sentence keeps the gap.
ops.new_text: Block-term tensor models offer one route to such a model. A block-term decomposition splits a multiway signal into blocks with low-rank factors per mode \cite{De_Lathauwer_2008}. In neural networks, block-term structure has compressed weight matrices, and those networks are explained with Grad-CAM maps instead of through their factors \cite{Ye_2020}. In supervised regression of brain signals, block-term tensor regression, designed for interpretability, predicted finger movements \cite{Faes_2024}. That regression is linear and has no survival objective, which incident prediction with censored follow-up needs. To our knowledge, no published model places readable block-term frequency and lead factors on the predictive path of a survival network for incident AF. Such a model would also need a way to add clinical risk factors, which complement the ECG \cite{Khurshid_2022}. The clinical factors should not enter the factors that are meant to be read, or the reading would mix the two sources.

ops.rationale: Names the 700-ECG sample of Valasakis_2026 (C76) and drops the binary contrast of the last sentence.
ops.new_text: This study addresses two questions. The first is whether a block-term tensor network predicts incident AF from one sinus-rhythm 12-lead ECG more accurately than a clinical risk-factor model and a convolutional neural network (CNN). In this network, the ECG evidence passes through readable frequency and lead factors. Age, sex and ECG intervals enter through a separate linear term. The second question is where in the cardiac cycle the ECG evidence of the network lies. We answer both questions in MIMIC-IV-ECG, with incident AF defined from hospital diagnoses coded in the International Classification of Diseases (ICD). Labels read from the ECG were not used as outcomes, since a third of a sample of 700 AF-labelled ECGs of this database did not show AF on expert review (Section~\ref{sec:cohort}) \cite{Valasakis_2026}. All methods share one cohort, one set of folds and one set of risk factors. Differences between them are therefore differences of model.

ops.rationale: Cuts the closing announcement of the four areas reviewed next.
ops.new_text:
The contributions of the study are these:
\begin{itemize}
\item BTTN, a survival network whose ECG evidence passes through per-block frequency and lead factors, with a separate linear clinical term that leaves those factors unchanged.
\item An incident-AF cohort in MIMIC-IV-ECG defined from ICD-coded hospital diagnoses with a 30-day blanking window, reported with its exclusion counts.
\item A comparison of one-year discrimination against a clinical model, a CNN and linear block-term tensor regression (BTTR) under one protocol, and the discrimination of one survival model at four horizons.
\item The calibration, risk stratification and operating points of BTTN with the clinical term.
\item A beat-aligned, energy-normalised occlusion profile of the ECG term of BTTN.
\end{itemize}

ops.rationale: Uses the wording C64 gives as supported for the Mayo Clinic network (454,789 ECGs in its training set) and states that the review groups models by confirmation window (C77).
ops.new_text: Two tasks are reported under the heading of AF prediction from the sinus-rhythm ECG, and they differ in what counts as a case. In identification, a case is a patient who already has AF or shows it soon after the ECG. A CNN developed on 649,931 sinus-rhythm ECGs of 180,922 Mayo Clinic patients, 454,789 of them in its training set, identified patients with AF with an AUC of 0.87, counting AF before the tested ECG as positive \cite{Attia_2019}. A network for AF within 31 days of a sinus-rhythm ECG reached AUROCs of 0.86 on held-out Veterans Affairs ECGs and 0.93 at a non-VA site \cite{Yuan_2023}. In incident prediction, a case is a patient whose first AF follows the ECG after a stated interval. The two tasks give different numbers. In a systematic review, models with 31-day confirmation windows had higher median AUCs than models with 1-year windows \cite{Tsiartas_2025}, and a narrative review found AI more accurate at shorter event horizons \cite{Saiz_Vivo_2025}. The present study addresses incident prediction only.

ops.rationale: Hedges the absence claim with 'To our knowledge' (C91) and cuts the two closing announcements, which also removes the section numbers typed by hand.
ops.new_text: The explanations in these studies are computed after training. Saliency mapping gave the P-wave the greatest influence in one ECG network \cite{Khurshid_2022}. Saliency of the image model focused on P-wave morphology and the PR interval \cite{Zeidaabadi_2026}. The feature-based model named lower P-wave amplitude among its predictors \cite{Riek_2026}. These reports agree on the atrial part of the beat. To our knowledge, none of these reports includes a test of whether the explanation reflects what the model uses to predict.

ops.rationale: Names the four kinds of input of the 0.909 model (C78).
ops.new_text: Studies that combined an ECG network with clinical factors found the two complementary in most cohorts. AUROC was comparable for CHARGE-AF and an ECG network in three test sets and highest for their combination, at 0.838, 0.777 and 0.746 \cite{Khurshid_2022}. In an older community cohort, an AI-ECG and CHARGE-AF had equal C statistics of 0.69, predicted AF independently, and reached 0.72 together \cite{Christopoulos_2020}. A single-lead ECG model with age and sex had an AUROC of 0.695 against 0.679 for CHARGE-AF in trial data \cite{Khurshid_2025}. A random forest that combined demographic, clinical, engineered and deep ECG features reached 0.909, against 0.839 for the best single modality \cite{Biton_2021}.

ops.rationale: Restores the source's hedge 'for most methods' (C73).
ops.new_text: Post-hoc explanations have been put to tests, and several methods fail them. Tests that randomise the model parameters and the training labels showed some saliency methods to be independent of both the model and the data-generating process \cite{arxiv_1810_03292}. Under remove-and-retrain evaluation, only VarGrad and SmoothGrad-Squared, of the methods tested, did better than a random assignment of importance \cite{arxiv_1806_10758}. On the ECG, twelve attribution methods agreed poorly with one another \cite{Arends_2026}. Their self-consistency across initialisations was moderate for most methods, with mean correlations of 0.41 to 0.65. Dataset-level auditing with sanity checks gives a more favourable reading, in which aggregated saliency aligned with the decision rules of cardiologists \cite{Wagner_2024}. In that work the same methods also supported knowledge discovery, such as subtypes of myocardial infarction. The balance of this evidence leaves any explanation computed after training open to doubt about what it shows. It motivates models whose readable parts lie on the path of the prediction itself.

ops.rationale: Reports the motor-imagery values as mean accuracies against higher-order discriminant analysis (C65), hedges the gap claim (C92) and cuts the closing announcement.
ops.new_text: Whether intrinsic interpretability costs accuracy on the ECG is contested. A study of variational-autoencoder representations of interpretable ECG features reported a cost of intrinsic explainability \cite{Patlatzoglou_2025}. A supervised block-term discriminant method reported none on EEG decoding, with a mean accuracy of 64.52\% against 61.00\% for its predecessor, higher-order discriminant analysis, on motor imagery \cite{arxiv_2511_04292}. Image networks that are interpretable by design also kept their accuracy \cite{arxiv_2205_10268,arxiv_2507_16761}. The answer may depend on the model family and on the task. To our knowledge, no study in this literature compares an intrinsically interpretable model with a CNN on incident AF under one protocol. That comparison is one aim of the present work.

ops.rationale: Cites Kolda_2009 for the CP and Tucker decompositions only (C79), states that Ye_2020 explains its networks with Grad-CAM (C74), and says the factors of this paper's model can be read, since no reading is reported.
ops.new_text: A block-term decomposition writes a tensor as a sum of blocks of low multilinear rank, and it contains the CP and Tucker decompositions as special cases \cite{De_Lathauwer_2008}. A survey covers the CP and Tucker decompositions \cite{Kolda_2009}. The uses of block-term structure differ in where the factors sit: in the weights of a network, within a recording, or on the input of a predictive model. Block-term tensor neural networks approximate the weight matrices of CNNs and recurrent networks by block-term tensors to compress them, and the networks are explained with Grad-CAM maps instead of through their factors \cite{Ye_2020}. The model of this paper shares part of that name and is a different model, whose factors act on the input and can be read. On AF ECGs, a regularised block-term decomposition extracted several signals interpretable as AF patterns \cite{Goulart_2020}. That work separates sources within a recording and does not predict risk.

ops.rationale: Ends the section on the gap sentence and cuts the announcement of the next section.
ops.new_text: Supervised block-term models extract factors that both predict and can be read. Block-term tensor regression (BTTR) predicted finger trajectories from intracranial recordings, with automatic extraction of its components \cite{Faes_2024}. A block-term discriminant analysis gave interpretable and efficient dimensionality reduction for brain-computer interfaces, with an ROC-AUC of 91.25\% on event-related potentials \cite{arxiv_2511_04292}. Linear BTTR has also been applied to the identification of AF in sinus rhythm on the median beat \cite{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22227432}, which is a different task from dated incidence. These models fit their blocks by deflation, score linearly, and have no time-to-event objective. No model in this literature trains readable block-term frequency and lead factors end to end with a survival objective for incident AF, with clinical factors kept outside the factor layer.

ops.rationale: Adds why the 50 Hz notch leaves 60 Hz mains outside the kept band, and states F = 21 bins (core/preprocess.py _spectral: nperseg 128 at 250 Hz, f <= 40 Hz keeps bins 0 to 20, 1.953 Hz apart).
ops.new_text: Each index ECG is a 10-second, 12-lead recording sampled at 500 Hz \cite{https://doi.org/10.13026/4nqg-sb35}. Each lead was high-pass filtered at 0.5 Hz with a second-order filter and notch filtered at 50 Hz. It was then denoised by soft thresholding of a three-level sym4 wavelet decomposition, decimated to 250 Hz, centred, and scaled by its maximum absolute value. A magnitude spectrogram was computed per lead with a 128-sample window (512 ms) and a 32-sample hop (128 ms). Frequencies up to 40 Hz were kept, magnitudes were transformed by $\log(1+x)$, and the time axis was resampled to 40 frames. Mains interference at 60 Hz, the mains frequency of the source hospital, therefore lies outside the kept band. The result is a tensor $\mathcal{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times T \times L}$ with $F = 21$ frequency bins from 0 to 39 Hz, 1.95 Hz apart, $T = 40$ time frames and $L = 12$ leads, standardised per recording. Within each training fold, each lead was standardised again with the statistics of the training patients. A magnitude spectrogram changes little when the beat shifts within a window, so beats need no alignment across recordings.

ops.rationale: Defines the mode-n product in the sentence and drops the citation to a passage not read (C68), and words the block-term comparison as the mode-n ranks the source characterises (C80).
Drops 'fitted by least squares', which the source does not state (C81), and words the factors of BTTN as factors that can be read.
ops.new_text: BTTN generalises linear BTTR \cite{Faes_2024}. Both models decompose the input into blocks with one factor per mode. BTTR fits its blocks one at a time by deflation, keeps a static score vector per block and predicts with a linear score. BTTN trains all blocks jointly by gradient descent and replaces the static score vector with learned temporal kernels. It pools their output, passes it through a nonlinear head and is fitted with a Cox survival objective. Figure~\ref{fig:bttr-to-bttn} shows the two models one above the other. The frequency and lead factors keep the same role in both models, so the factors of BTTN can be read as those of BTTR can.

ops.rationale: Describes the attention pooling as one set of weights over time computed from all channels and shared by them (core/bttn.py: attn = Conv1d(ch_out, 1, 1), softmax over time).
ops.new_text: The 72 time series of the block-term layer pass through depthwise temporal convolutions at three scales. Each series is convolved with six kernels of each of the lengths 3, 7 and 15 frames, so that each output channel depends on one series of one block. Batch normalisation and a rectified linear unit follow. Each channel is then pooled along time in two ways: by one set of attention weights over time, computed from all channels by a softmax and shared by them, and by its maximum. The two pooled vectors are concatenated. A head with two hidden layers of 256 and 128 units, batch normalisation, rectified linear units and dropout of 0.4 maps the pooled vector to a scalar log-risk $\eta_{\mathrm{ECG}}$. This network without clinical factors is the ECG term of BTTN, called ECG-only BTTN when it is evaluated alone.

ops.rationale: Removes the clause that other AF survival models use the Cox likelihood, which the cited discrete-time model does not (C66); 2.1 already states that model's loss.

Ties 'readable' to the 'interpretable' of the title, states that no reading of the learned factors is reported, and cuts the closing announcement.
ops.new_text: This construction makes the factors readable by design and keeps the clinical term out of them. In this paper, readable names this property of the factors of a model that is interpretable by design. It is the sense in which the title calls BTTN interpretable. Every path from the ECG to the risk passes through the block projections of Equation~\eqref{eq:block}. The frequency and lead factors are therefore parameters on which the prediction depends, and they can be read directly. The clinical term reaches the log-risk without passing through the block-term layer. Adding it leaves the role of the factors unchanged, and the risk factors can be read as a linear term beside the ECG evidence. Readability is here a property of the architecture, and this study reports no reading of the learned frequency and lead factors. Whether the nonlinear head uses the factors in the way a reader of them would assume is a separate question, which this study does not measure \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}.

ops.new_text: The one-year comparison used stratified five-fold cross-validation at the patient level, repeated over five seeds, with each patient's scores averaged over seeds. The survival model used one stratified five-fold split, with an event within one year as the label for early stopping. AUROC intervals come from 2,000 bootstrap resamples with percentile limits. At each horizon, cases had an event by the horizon and controls were AF-free beyond it, and patients censored earlier were excluded. Calibration and clinical use were assessed at one year in the survival sample, after two-fold cross-fitted logistic recalibration. They were measured by Brier scores, decision curves \cite{Vickers_2006} and operating points at the top 5, 10, 20 and 30\% of risk. Positive predictive value (PPV) and the number needed to monitor, its inverse, were recomputed at the proportion of cases among the cases and AF-free controls of the one-year design, 1,855 in 43,625. We report the study with reference to the TRIPOD+AI statement \cite{Collins_2024}, without a table of participant characteristics and without counts of missing values per clinical factor.

ops.new_text: The offsets were grouped into five windows relative to the R peak, the P, PR, QRS, ST and T windows. Table~\ref{tab:occlusion} gives the offsets each window contains and the span of the beat that their occlusions cover. These windows are fixed offsets and are not delineated per beat. A negative mean drop at a lead and offset was set to zero before the window means were taken, for both the raw and the normalised value. The profile of a window is the mean over leads and over the offsets it contains. The replacement value and the window size shape an occlusion map \cite{arxiv_1702_04595}, and the perturbation method and the region size shape the evaluation of attributions on time series \cite{_imi__2025}. The zero replacement and the 25 ms window are therefore choices of this readout. The readout describes the fitted model on its own training ECGs.

ops.new_text: Of 151,941 patients with an eligible sinus-rhythm index ECG, 1,855 developed incident AF within one year and 41,770 qualified as controls (Table~\ref{tab:cohort}). The survival design held 8,775 events with the same 41,770 controls. The exclusion categories were counted over all eligible patients and overlap. The table therefore lists each count against the eligible total. Incident events numbered 1,855, 2,828 and 5,262 by one, two and five years. Controls had a median follow-up of 1,601 days (interquartile range 880 to 2,559). Of the controls, 40,960 (98.1\%) had an ECG after the index ECG. For 40,306 (96.5\%), the last of these ECGs was not read as AF.

ops.new_text: One survival model gave the fused model an AUROC of 0.723 [0.701, 0.745] at 120 days, for onset in the 90 days after the blanking window, 31 to 120 days after the index ECG (Table~\ref{tab:horizons}). Its AUROC was 0.727 [0.711, 0.743] at one year, 0.740 [0.727, 0.753] at two years and 0.745 [0.735, 0.755] at five years. The clinical Cox model had point estimates of 0.710, 0.711, 0.727 and 0.731, below those of the fused model at each horizon. ECG-only BTTN ranged from 0.658 to 0.676. The four horizons share one model and overlapping patients. They describe the behaviour of one model and are not independent replications. One reason for the lower one-year values of the survival design is its control group. At one year it includes patients who develop AF later, whereas the controls of the one-year design have no AF diagnosis.

ops.new_text:
After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, predicted and observed one-year proportions agreed across deciles of the fused model, among 19,986 patients with 838 cases (Figure~\ref{fig:clinical-utility}). The deciles are read in that sample, which holds a larger share of the events of the cohort than of its controls (4,000 of 8,775 against 16,000 of 41,770). Its proportions of AF are therefore higher than those of the cohort. Observed one-year AF rose from 0.55\% in the lowest decile to 11.4\% in the highest, with mean predicted risks of 0.61\% and 12.3\%. The sixth and seventh deciles (bars 5 and 6 of Figure~\ref{fig:clinical-utility}, 4.95\% and 4.15\%) were inverted. Brier scores were 0.0390 for the fused model, 0.0396 for ECG-only BTTN and 0.0398 for the clinical model.

At the top 10\% of risk, the fused model had a sensitivity of 0.272 against 0.240 for the clinical model, at specificities of 0.908 and 0.906 (Table~\ref{tab:operating}). At the proportion of cases in the one-year design, its PPV was 0.1155 against 0.1019, a number needed to monitor of 8.7 against 9.8. Sensitivity and PPV were higher for the fused model than for the clinical model at all four flagged fractions.

The thresholds in this paragraph are read from the decision curves of Figure~\ref{fig:clinical-utility}. All three models had a net benefit above both treating all and treating none at threshold probabilities from about 0.04 to about 0.1. Below about 0.04, their curves lay close to that of treating all. The curve of the fused model lay above the other two between about 0.03 and 0.12, and all curves lay near zero above about 0.12.

ops.new_text: Raw occlusion of the ECG term was dominated by the QRS window, where the mean drop in log-risk was 0.0232 against 0.0037 in the PR window (Table~\ref{tab:occlusion}). The QRS complex has the highest amplitude of the beat, so zeroing it removes the most energy and changes the spectrogram most. Per unit of energy removed, the profile was highest in the PR window, at 0.00216. The ST window (0.00157), the P window (0.00152) and the T window (0.00127) followed, and the QRS window was lowest (0.00086). The P and ST windows were close to each other. Figure~\ref{fig:beat-saliency} shows the energy-normalised response on the mean median beat of each lead. The profile describes what the fitted ECG term responds to on 120 high-risk training ECGs.

ops.new_text: Four results answer the research question within one health system. BTTN with the clinical term had the highest one-year discrimination of the methods compared. Its point estimates stayed above those of the clinical model at four horizons read from one survival model. Its ECG term alone was comparable to a CNN under the same protocol. After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, the predicted and observed one-year proportions of the fused model agreed across risk deciles. It flagged more future cases than the clinical model at each flagged fraction. Per unit of energy, its ECG term responded most to the PR window of the beat. The one-year interval of the fused model overlaps that of the clinical model. Its gain over the clinical model is therefore small and consistent in direction, and it is not established as a difference by an interval of its own.

ops.rationale: Drops the horizon the source does not give for 0.77 (C69), ties the 0.996 to a benchmark on MIMIC-IV-ECG as the abstract does (C83), and drops the binary contrast of the topic sentence.
ops.new_text: Published results give context for these values. On the hospital behind MIMIC-IV, a survival-loss CNN reached a C-index of 0.750 \cite{Sau_2026} and an image-based model 0.754 \cite{Zeidaabadi_2026}. A Montreal model reached an AUROC of 0.77 on external validation in MIMIC-IV, with a label source that its abstract does not state \cite{Jabbour_2024}. Elsewhere, an AUROC of 0.85 at one year \cite{Raghunath_2021} and a C-index of 0.781 over a short follow-up \cite{Riek_2026} were reported. These studies differ from the present one in horizon, outcome definition, sample and metric. A systematic review shows how far such choices move reported values \cite{Tsiartas_2025}. Identification studies \cite{Attia_2019,Yuan_2023} address another task. So does AF diagnosis: a foundation model evaluated with a benchmark on MIMIC-IV-ECG reported an AUROC of 0.996 for AF \cite{McKeen_2025}.

ops.rationale: States the property as architectural: an ECG term built on readable factors.
ops.new_text: The gain of the fused model over the clinical model agrees with reports that ECG and clinical information are complementary \cite{Khurshid_2022,Christopoulos_2020}. Its operating point at the top 10\% of risk is of the same order as that of one externally validated model. That model flagged 9.7\% of older patients with a sensitivity of 31\% and a specificity of 92\%, in a different population with chart-confirmed endpoints \cite{Pfeifer_2026}. The comparability of ECG-only BTTN with the CNN bears on the reported accuracy cost of intrinsic interpretability on the ECG \cite{Patlatzoglou_2025}. In this design, the ECG term built on readable factors reached the discrimination of a compact CNN. The CNN has three convolutional layers, so the result says nothing about parity with the large networks of published work.

ops.rationale: Replaces 'A reader can therefore inspect the two sources apart' by the architectural statement and says that no reading of the fitted factors is reported.
ops.new_text: Separating the clinical term from the block-term layer lets the fused model gain discrimination without changing what its ECG factors mean. The ECG evidence still passes through frequency and lead factors, and each risk factor enters the linear term with one weight. The two sources therefore have separate parameters that can be inspected apart, although this study reports no reading of the fitted frequency and lead factors. In a fused network whose clinical inputs enter the factor layer, the factors could absorb risk-factor information, as concept representations absorb information beyond their concepts \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}. The architecture of BTTN closes this route for the clinical term. It does not close it for information that the ECG itself carries, which the factors may encode in ways a reader does not expect.

ops.rationale: Gives each P-wave source its own clause so the meta-analysis has an antecedent.
ops.new_text: The PR-window concentration of the occlusion profile is in line with saliency reports of other incident-AF models. These pointed to the P-wave \cite{Khurshid_2022} and to P-wave morphology and the PR interval \cite{Zeidaabadi_2026}. It is also in line with cohort studies that tie the PR interval measured in sinus rhythm to later AF. In Framingham, the PR interval was a predictor in the AF risk score \cite{Schnabel_2009}, and first-degree atrioventricular block carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.06 \cite{Cheng_2009}. Each standard deviation of the PR interval carried a hazard ratio of 1.13 in older Black and White adults \cite{Magnani_2013}. First-degree block carried a hazard ratio of 1.75 in an older Japanese population \cite{Tanaka_2021}. In Black adults of the Jackson Heart Study, the PR interval, P-wave duration and P-wave terminal force were each associated with AF \cite{Yogeswaran_2025}. P-wave indices show the same direction in a two-cohort study \cite{Magnani_2015} and in a meta-analysis whose evidence was of very low certainty in selected populations \cite{Emmanuela_2026}.

ops.rationale: Gives the PR window's centres and occluded span in place of the grouping boundaries, and states what the span holds on the mean beat of Figure 3 (lead II: P wave returns to baseline near 110 ms before the R peak).
ops.new_text: The association is not uniform, and the comparison has a limited scope. In a Swedish cohort of 70-year-olds, the PR interval measured in lead V1 was not related to incident AF, while a short P-wave duration was \cite{Ostrowska_2022}. The cohort studies measure the PR interval from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex. The PR window of the readout groups the occlusions centred 125 to 75 ms before the R peak, a fixed span from about 138 to 63 ms before it. On the mean beat of Figure~\ref{fig:beat-saliency}, this span holds the end of the P wave and the PR segment. The agreement claimed here therefore concerns the location within the cardiac cycle only. The clinical term holds P-wave duration but no PR interval. One reading of the gain of the fused model is that the ECG term carries information on atrial and atrioventricular conduction that the clinical term does not measure. The present results do not test this reading, which remains a hypothesis.

ops.rationale: Uses the consensus's working definition with its clinically relevant manifestations (C84).
ops.new_text: An atrial focus also has a clinical frame. An expert consensus defines atrial cardiomyopathy as structural, architectural, contractile or electrophysiological changes of the atria that can produce clinically relevant manifestations, among them arrhythmia \cite{Goette_2016}. In a Japanese community cohort, prolonged P-wave duration was associated both with incident AF and with more left atrial fibrosis at autopsy \cite{Maezono_2025}. One reading of the PR-window response is that it reflects such atrial change. The readout cannot show this. The reading is offered as a hypothesis for studies that pair the ECG with measurements of the atrium.

ops.rationale: Moves the PPV sentence into a new limitations paragraph on the evaluation that states the in-sample recalibration, that the one-year design's case proportion (1,855 in 43,625) exceeds the survival cohort's one-year rate (1,855 in 50,545, Table 1) so the PPVs are upper values, and that no characteristics table is reported.
ops.new_text:
The comparator and the covariates have limits of their own. Age is the anchor age of MIMIC-IV, which is not the age at the index ECG \cite{Johnson_2023}. The clinical factors omit variables of the Framingham score, among them systolic blood pressure, hypertension treatment, body mass index and heart failure \cite{Schnabel_2009}. They also omit the PR interval, a known AF predictor \cite{Cheng_2009,Magnani_2013}. The clinical comparator is therefore narrower than a full clinical score. The CNN is compact, and a larger network might reach a different value.

The evaluation of calibration and operating points has limits as well. The probabilities were recalibrated in the evaluation sample with two-fold cross-fitting, so the calibration of the model in another population is not shown. The one-year design sampled four controls per case, and the survival design sampled cases and controls. PPV was therefore recomputed at the proportion of cases among the cases and AF-free controls of the one-year design, 1,855 in 43,625. This proportion exceeds the one-year rate of the survival cohort, 1,855 in 50,545, whose controls include the patients with onset after one year. The PPVs of Table~\ref{tab:operating} are therefore upper values for that population. The study also reports no table of the characteristics of cases and controls and no count of missing values per clinical factor. The sample therefore cannot be compared with another population on these measures.

ops.rationale: Cites each occlusion source for what it holds, as in 4.3 (C82).
ops.new_text: The occlusion readout is a perturbation explanation of the fitted model on 120 high-risk training ECGs. It is open to the critiques of post-hoc attribution \cite{arxiv_1810_03292,arxiv_1806_10758,Arends_2026}. Its zero replacement, its 25 ms window and its fixed windows relative to the R peak shape the profile, since the replacement value and the window size shape an occlusion map \cite{arxiv_1702_04595}. The perturbation method and the region size likewise shape the evaluation of attributions on time series \cite{_imi__2025}. Another replacement could change the order of the windows. Readable factors do not by themselves show that the nonlinear head routes its decision through them in the way their reading suggests \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}. The readability of BTTN rests on its architecture, and this study reports no measurement of how far the factors carry the decision on ICD-coded labels.

ops.rationale: Cites remove-and-retrain evaluation for the removal test and TRIPOD+AI for the reporting of external validation (C103), both read in this run.
ops.new_text: Several studies would extend this work. A test of the block factors on ICD-coded labels would measure how far the factors carry the decision. It would use control probes and the removal of top-ranked against bottom-ranked factors, in the manner of remove-and-retrain evaluation \cite{arxiv_1806_10758}. External validation in a cohort with dated outcomes, and temporal validation within MIMIC-IV, would test whether the model transports. Such validation would be reported with reference to the TRIPOD+AI statement \cite{Collins_2024}. A clinical comparator that includes the PR interval and the variables of a full clinical score would sharpen the comparison with the clinical model. A paired interval for the difference between the fused and the clinical model would show whether the one-year gain exceeds sampling variation. An occlusion readout on held-out ECGs, with replacements other than zero, would show how far the PR-window profile depends on the choices of the present readout.

ops.rationale: Keeps the decile statement with its recalibration qualifier in place of 'calibrated', labels the shortest horizon 120 days from the index ECG, and rewords the closing contrast.
ops.new_text: On ICD-coded labels in MIMIC-IV-ECG, a block-term tensor network with a separate clinical term had the highest one-year discrimination of the methods compared. Its AUROC was 0.7776, against 0.7597 for a clinical model and 0.7350 for a CNN. One survival model kept its point estimates above those of the clinical model at horizons from 120 days to five years after the index ECG. After logistic recalibration within the survival sample, the predicted and observed one-year proportions of the fused model agreed across risk deciles. The fused model also flagged more future cases than the clinical model at each flagged fraction. Its gain over the clinical model is small, and the one-year intervals overlap. The gain is consistent in direction within one health system, and no interval for the difference yet establishes it.

ops.rationale: Replaces 'keeps its ECG evidence readable' by the architectural statement that the evidence passes through factors on the predictive path that can be read.
ops.new_text: The ECG term alone reached the discrimination of a compact CNN under the same protocol, while its evidence passes through frequency and lead factors that lie on the predictive path and can be read. The clinical term adds the risk factors without passing through those factors. The fused model thus gains discrimination while its ECG evidence still passes through those factors. Per unit of signal energy, the ECG term responded most to the PR window of the beat. This is the part of the cardiac cycle that cohort studies of the PR interval tie to later AF \cite{Cheng_2009,Magnani_2013}. The readout describes the fitted model, and its atrial reading remains a hypothesis.

ops.rationale: Rewrites the first sentence to what the results show: a model whose ECG evidence passes through block-term factors reached the discrimination of a compact CNN.
ops.new_text: For the design of ECG risk models, a model whose ECG evidence passes through block-term factors reached the discrimination of a compact CNN on this task. The results also suggest that clinical factors can be added beside such factors without entering them. The clinical comparator used here is narrower than a full clinical score, and the readout is descriptive. Validation outside one health system, a test of the factors on ICD-coded labels and a comparator that includes the PR interval are the next requirements before any clinical use.
